::: {.callout-note title="Before you start"}
Complete [Add size distributions](sans-size-distributions.qmd) first.
Use the same environment and run from `docs/tutorials` in a repository checkout.
This final step retains the pySEB particle and uses **sasmodels, the modelling
library used by SasView**, for interactions and resolution smearing.
:::

We have fitted the same data twice: first with identical droplets, then with
a size distribution. The remaining mismatch asks a different question:
**are independently scattering particles and a perfectly sharp instrument
response adequate?**

Here we add an effective hard-sphere interaction and an approximate resolution
correction. At the end, one interactive viewer brings the three fits together.
The 3D particle, intensity curves and residuals change with the selected stage.

## Continue from the size-distribution fit

The folded setup rebuilds the preceding calculations in a fresh kernel,
without rerunning their plots or opening their viewers.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Rebuild the first two fits"
from _aot_setup import previous_stage

globals().update(previous_stage("distributions"))
```

## Include the surrounding droplets and instrument response


This extends the same pySEB particle used on the first two pages. pySEB
supplies the linked particle's scattering expression; sasmodels supplies
interactions and resolution, and SciPy fits the parameters. sasmodels also averages the particle population. The adapter connects these
components through the optional `pyseb.sasmodels` interface. The fitting
choices remain explicit in this tutorial. See the
[sasmodels resolution API](https://www.sasview.org/docs/dev/sasmodels-api/resolution.html)
for the measurement interface.

Size distributions smooth the form-factor minima, but do not account for
correlations between droplet positions. At a volume fraction around 6%,
the dilute-particle assumption deserves a test. A
[Percus–Yevick hard-sphere structure factor](https://www.sasview.org/docs/user/models/hardsphere.html)
provides a simple model of excluded-volume repulsion.

For a polydisperse population we use the **decoupling approximation**:

$$
I(q)=\frac{\phi}{\langle V\rangle}10^8
\left[\langle F(q)^2\rangle+
\langle F(q)\rangle^2\{S(q)-1\}\right]+B.
$$

Here $F=\beta_c A_c+\beta_s A_s$ is the signed amplitude of our linked
structure. Averaging the signed amplitude matters: simply multiplying the
averaged intensity by $S(q)$ neglects the contrast-dependent correction for
size dispersity. This approximation neglects correlations between particle
size and position; it is not an exact mixture structure factor.

We add one shared parameter, the effective interaction packing fraction
$\eta$. The hard-sphere radius is fixed to
$(3\langle V\rangle/4\pi)^{1/3}$. We keep $\eta$ separate from the absolute
intensity's volume fraction $\phi$: this tests an effective interaction model,
not a strictly self-consistent hard-sphere fluid. A successful fit does not
establish a microscopic interaction potential.

We also include a fixed Gaussian resolution with standard deviation
$\sigma_q=0.10q$, following the approximate resolution assumed in the
[source tutorial](https://www.sasview.org/downloads/simultaneous_1d_fitting_in_sasview_v6.pdf).
The files contain no measured resolution widths, so this remains an assumption.
We use sasmodels `Pinhole1D` with its default finite Gaussian window
(2.5 standard deviations below and 3 above each measured q), rather than an
unbounded Gaussian convolution.
Resolution is applied to the complete interacting intensity before comparison
with the data. All 363 selected measurements and their original uncertainties
remain in the objective.

### Evaluate the population and structure factor

sasmodels composes our particle with `hardsphere`. We explicitly select
`structure_factor_mode=1` for the decoupling approximation. Its product model
normally uses the same volume fraction for interaction strength and absolute
intensity. Here the effective packing fraction remains independent: we set
`volfraction=eta` and `scale=phi/eta`. At zero eta we use the particle directly.
The effective radius is calculated from the library's averaged particle volume,
preserving the radius convention used above.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Evaluate the pySEB particle through sasmodels"
interaction_info = with_hardsphere(particle_spec, backend="compiled")
interaction_model = build_model(interaction_info, platform="dll", dtype="double")


@lru_cache(maxsize=16)
def interaction_kernel(q_values):
    return interaction_model.make_kernel([np.asarray(q_values)])


@lru_cache(maxsize=16)
def measurement_resolution(q_values, resolution_points=3000):
    q = np.asarray(q_values)
    q_calc = np.geomspace(0.7 * q.min(), 1.4 * q.max(), resolution_points)
    return Pinhole1D(q, 0.10 * q, q_calc=q_calc)


def interacting_intensity(contrast, q, values, background,
                          population_points=41, resolution_points=3000):
    radius, thickness, radius_sd, thickness_sd, phi = values[:5]
    eta = values[8]
    parameters = population_parameters(
        contrast, radius, thickness, radius_sd, thickness_sd, population_points,
    )
    resolution = measurement_resolution(tuple(q), resolution_points)
    if eta == 0:
        theory = call_kernel(particle_kernel(tuple(resolution.q_calc)), dict(
            parameters, scale=phi, background=0.0,
        ))
    else:
        _, _, _, mean_volume, _ = call_Fq(
            particle_kernel((0.01,)), parameters.copy(),
        )
        theory = call_kernel(interaction_kernel(tuple(resolution.q_calc)), dict(
            parameters, radius_effective=(3 * mean_volume / (4 * np.pi))**(1/3),
            volfraction=eta, scale=phi/eta, background=0.0,
            structure_factor_mode=1, radius_effective_mode=0,
        ))
    return resolution.apply(theory) + background
```

### Fit the same data with one additional variable

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Fit interactions and resolution"
def interacting_residual_vector(values, **quadrature):
    return np.concatenate([
        (interacting_intensity(
            contrast, datasets[contrast]["q"], values, values[5 + index],
            **quadrature,
        ) - datasets[contrast]["intensity"]) / datasets[contrast]["uncertainty"]
        for index, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order)
    ])


interaction_lower = np.r_[disperse_lower, 0.0]
interaction_upper = np.r_[disperse_upper, 0.3]
interaction_fit = least_squares(
    interacting_residual_vector,
    np.r_[disperse_fit.x, 0.05],
    bounds=(interaction_lower, interaction_upper),
    x_scale="jac",
)
assert interaction_fit.success, interaction_fit.message
interaction_chi_squared = np.sum(interaction_fit.fun**2) / (
    interaction_fit.fun.size - interaction_fit.x.size
)
for name, value in zip(
    (*disperse_parameter_names, "interaction packing fraction"), interaction_fit.x,
):
    print(f"{name:30s} {value:.6g}")
print(f"interacting reduced chi-squared {interaction_chi_squared:.3f}")

for label, result in (
    ("monodisperse", fit), ("size distributions", disperse_fit),
    ("interactions + resolution", interaction_fit),
):
    chi2 = np.sum(result.fun**2)
    print(f"{label:26s} k={result.x.size:2d}  "
          f"chi2/dof={chi2 / (result.fun.size - result.x.size):.3f}  "
          f"AIC={chi2 + 2 * result.x.size:.1f}")
```

AIC here omits the common constant for independent Gaussian observations with
known uncertainties. It penalizes added parameters, but a lower AIC does not
prove the model is physically correct.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Numerical checks and static plots"}

We compare the adapter with an independent sasmodels core-shell model at
all three contrasts, check the zero-dispersity and zero-interaction limits,
and double the distribution and resolution grids. Integration error should
be small compared with the measured uncertainties.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Check numerical limits and integration grids"
from sasmodels.core import load_model

check_q = datasets["Core"]["q"]
reference_model = load_model("core_shell_sphere", platform="dll", dtype="double")
reference_kernel = reference_model.make_kernel([check_q])
for index, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order):
    parameters = population_parameters(contrast, *interaction_fit.x[:4])
    expected = call_kernel(reference_kernel, dict(parameters, scale=1., background=0.))
    actual = call_kernel(particle_kernel(tuple(check_q)), dict(parameters, scale=1., background=0.))
    np.testing.assert_allclose(actual, expected, rtol=1e-7, atol=1e-8)

    radius, thickness = interaction_fit.x[:2]
    rc, rs, solvent = sld[contrast]
    vc = 4 * np.pi * radius**3 / 3
    vo = 4 * np.pi * (radius + thickness)**3 / 3
    native = world.EvaluateFormFactorUnnormalized("droplet", {
        "R_core": radius, "Ri_shell": radius, "Ro_shell": radius + thickness,
        "beta_core": (rc-solvent)*1e-6*vc,
        "beta_shell": (rs-solvent)*1e-6*(vo-vc),
    }, check_q.tolist())
    mono = calculate_disperse_intensity(contrast, check_q, radius, thickness, 0, 0, 1, 0)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(mono, np.asarray(native)*1e8/vo, rtol=1e-7, atol=1e-8)

    tiny_eta = interaction_fit.x.copy()
    tiny_eta[8] = 1e-10
    zero_eta = interaction_fit.x.copy()
    zero_eta[8] = 0
    resolution = measurement_resolution(tuple(check_q))
    unsmeared = calculate_disperse_intensity(contrast, resolution.q_calc, *zero_eta[:5], 0.)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(interacting_intensity(contrast, check_q, zero_eta, 0.),
                               resolution.apply(unsmeared), rtol=1e-12)
    np.testing.assert_allclose(interacting_intensity(contrast, check_q, tiny_eta, 0.),
                               resolution.apply(unsmeared), rtol=1e-8)
reference_kernel.release()
reference_model.release()
np.testing.assert_allclose(resolution.apply(np.ones_like(resolution.q_calc)), 1)
np.testing.assert_allclose(Perfect1D(check_q).apply(check_q**2), check_q**2)
fine_residual = interacting_residual_vector(
    interaction_fit.x, population_points=81, resolution_points=6000,
)
disperse_fine = np.concatenate([
    (calculate_disperse_intensity(
        contrast, datasets[contrast]["q"], *disperse_fit.x[:5],
        disperse_fit.x[5 + index], population_points=81,
    ) - datasets[contrast]["intensity"]) / datasets[contrast]["uncertainty"]
    for index, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order)
])
assert np.max(np.abs(disperse_fine - disperse_fit.fun)) < 0.05
quadrature_error = np.max(np.abs(fine_residual - interaction_fit.fun))
print(f"Largest integration change / measured uncertainty: {quadrature_error:.4g}")
assert quadrature_error < 0.05
```

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Plot all contrasts and residuals"
#| label: fig-real-aot-interacting-fit
#| fig-cap: "Shared geometry with hard-sphere interactions and approximate resolution smearing. Dashed curves show the noninteracting size-distribution fit."

figure, axes = plt.subplots(3, 2, figsize=(10, 10), sharex="col")
for index, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order):
    data = datasets[contrast]
    prediction = interacting_intensity(
        contrast, data["q"], interaction_fit.x, interaction_fit.x[5 + index],
    )
    previous = calculate_disperse_intensity(
        contrast, data["q"], *disperse_fit.x[:5], disperse_fit.x[5 + index],
    )
    positive = data["intensity"] > 0
    axes[index, 0].errorbar(
        data["q"][positive], data["intensity"][positive],
        yerr=data["uncertainty"][positive], fmt=".", markersize=3,
        label="measurement",
    )
    axes[index, 0].plot(data["q"], previous, "--", color="grey", label="noninteracting")
    axes[index, 0].plot(data["q"], prediction, label="interactions + resolution")
    axes[index, 0].set(xscale="log", yscale="log", ylabel=f"{contrast}\n$I(q)$ (cm$^{{-1}}$)")
    axes[index, 0].legend(fontsize="small")
    residual = (data["intensity"] - prediction) / data["uncertainty"]
    axes[index, 1].plot(data["q"], residual, ".", markersize=3)
    for level in (-2, 0, 2):
        axes[index, 1].axhline(level, color="grey", linewidth=0.7)
    axes[index, 1].set(xscale="log", ylabel="residual / uncertainty")
    print(f"{contrast}: mean squared normalized residual = {np.mean(residual**2):.3f}")
for axis in axes[-1]:
    axis.set_xlabel(r"$q$ (Å$^{-1}$)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

:::

The reduced chi-squared falls from **29.50** for the monodisperse model to
**20.49** with size distributions and **1.83** with interactions and sasmodels resolution.
The final fit has nine parameters, compared with eight for the noninteracting
size-distribution model. The core radius is about **25.2 Å**, shell thickness
**8.6 Å**, core relative width **0.158**, and shell relative width **0.366**.
The shared volume fraction is about **0.0596** and effective interaction packing
fraction about **0.0762**.

## Explore the whole fitting story

Use the selector to move from **identical droplets**, through **a size
population**, to **interactions and resolution**. The same three measurements
stay visible. The particle geometry and all predicted curves and residuals
update together; the title reports the fit score at that stage.

The 3D view shows one representative core–shell particle at the fitted size
parameters. It does not display the full size distribution or simulate the
spatial arrangement of interacting droplets. Rotate the particle to inspect
the core through the translucent surfactant shell.

```{python}
#| code-fold: true
#| code-summary: "Build the interactive comparison of all three fitting stages"
import plotly.graph_objects as go
from plotly.subplots import make_subplots

stages = [
    ("Identical droplets", fit, reduced_chi_squared),
    ("Size distributions", disperse_fit, disperse_reduced_chi_squared),
    ("Interactions + resolution", interaction_fit, interaction_chi_squared),
]
colors = {"Core": "#247ba0", "Drop": "#d1495b", "Shell": "#39875b"}
viewer = make_subplots(
    rows=3, cols=3,
    specs=[[{"type": "scene", "rowspan": 3}, {}, {}],
           [None, {}, {}], [None, {}, {}]],
    column_widths=[0.35, 0.43, 0.22],
    subplot_titles=("Representative droplet", "Intensity", "Residual / uncertainty",
                    "", "", "", ""),
    horizontal_spacing=0.06, vertical_spacing=0.08,
)
measurement_traces = []
for row, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order, 1):
    data = datasets[contrast]
    positive = data["intensity"] > 0
    measurement_traces.append(len(viewer.data))
    viewer.add_trace(go.Scatter(
        x=data["q"][positive], y=data["intensity"][positive],
        error_y=dict(type="data", array=data["uncertainty"][positive],
                     thickness=0.6, width=0, color="#888888"),
        mode="markers", marker=dict(size=3, color=colors[contrast], opacity=0.65),
        name=f"{contrast} data", legendgroup=contrast,
    ), row=row, col=2)
    viewer.update_xaxes(type="log", title_text="q [Å⁻¹]" if row == 3 else None,
                        row=row, col=2)
    viewer.update_yaxes(type="log", title_text=f"{contrast} I(q) [cm⁻¹]", row=row, col=2)
    viewer.update_xaxes(type="log", title_text="q [Å⁻¹]" if row == 3 else None,
                        row=row, col=3)
    viewer.update_yaxes(title_text=contrast, row=row, col=3)
    for level in (-2, 0, 2):
        viewer.add_hline(y=level, line_width=1, line_color="#999999",
                         line_dash="solid" if level == 0 else "dot", row=row, col=3)

stage_traces = []
for index, (label, result, score) in enumerate(stages):
    indices = []
    radius_value, thickness_value = map(float, result.x[:2])
    geometry = dict(R_core=radius_value, Ri_shell=radius_value,
                    Ro_shell=radius_value + thickness_value)
    options = pyseb.USDExportOptions(pyseb.LengthUnit.Angstrom)
    options.opacity_overrides = {"shell": 0.25}
    options.color_overrides = {"core": (0.15, 0.48, 0.65), "shell": (0.9, 0.65, 0.25)}
    particle_view = pyseb.structure_figure(world, "droplet", geometry, options, layouts=["random", "readable"])
    for trace in particle_view.data:
        indices.append(len(viewer.data))
        trace.visible = index == 2
        trace.showlegend = False
        viewer.add_trace(trace, row=1, col=1)
    for row, contrast in enumerate(contrast_order, 1):
        data = datasets[contrast]
        if index == 0:
            prediction = calculate_intensity(contrast, data["q"], *result.x[:3], result.x[2 + row])
        elif index == 1:
            prediction = calculate_disperse_intensity(contrast, data["q"], *result.x[:5], result.x[4 + row])
        else:
            prediction = interacting_intensity(contrast, data["q"], result.x, result.x[4 + row])
        indices.append(len(viewer.data))
        viewer.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=data["q"], y=prediction, mode="lines", line=dict(color=colors[contrast]),
            visible=index == 2, name=f"{contrast} fit", showlegend=False,
        ), row=row, col=2)
        indices.append(len(viewer.data))
        viewer.add_trace(go.Scatter(
            x=data["q"], y=(data["intensity"] - prediction)/data["uncertainty"],
            mode="markers", marker=dict(size=3, color=colors[contrast]),
            visible=index == 2, showlegend=False, name=f"{contrast} residual",
        ), row=row, col=3)
    stage_traces.append(indices)

buttons = []
for index, (label, result, score) in enumerate(stages):
    visible = [i in measurement_traces or i in stage_traces[index]
               for i in range(len(viewer.data))]
    title = (f"{label}: reduced χ² = {score:.2f} · "
             f"core R = {result.x[0]:.2f} Å · shell thickness = {result.x[1]:.2f} Å")
    buttons.append(dict(label=label, method="update",
                        args=[{"visible": visible}, {"title.text": title}]))
viewer.update_layout(
    height=800, margin=dict(l=20, r=20, t=135, b=30),
    title=dict(text=buttons[2]["args"][1]["title.text"], x=0.02, y=0.99,
               xanchor="left", yanchor="top", font=dict(size=14)),
    updatemenus=[dict(buttons=buttons, active=2, x=0, y=1.10, xanchor="left")],
    scene=dict(aspectmode="data", xaxis=dict(visible=False),
               yaxis=dict(visible=False), zaxis=dict(visible=False),
               camera=dict(eye=dict(x=1.8, y=1.8, z=1.5))),
    uirevision="aot-fit-story", legend=dict(orientation="h", y=-0.08),
)
from IPython.display import HTML, display

# Quarto already renders the page's mathematics. Avoid loading MathJax twice.
display(HTML(viewer.to_html(
    full_html=False, include_plotlyjs=True, include_mathjax=False,
    config={"displaylogo": False, "responsive": True},
)))
```

The largest improvement comes in the final step: reduced χ² falls from
**29.50 → 20.49 → 1.83**. The 3D particle remains a core and a shell throughout;
what changes is the description of its population and measurement. The final
fit uses **pySEB for particle scattering, sasmodels for distributions,
interactions and resolution, and SciPy for optimization**.

This comparison adds interactions and resolution together. It demonstrates
their combined effect; it does not establish how much of the improvement
comes from either contribution separately.

The shell-contrast background reaches its lower bound of zero. Residuals still
show some mismatch, and the resolution was assumed rather than measured. These
are reasons to avoid treating the fitted geometry as a unique solution or
reporting precision based only on the optimizer's local curvature. The next
experimental checks would be measured resolution, background subtraction, and
whether the same interaction model is adequate at other concentrations.
